175:The range means one specific thing and the chip's label says which: **how sure we are of the number, not how much the world can move.** That label, and the sentence behind it on hover, are written out word for word in `tiles-ports-wires.md`.
181:**A map is not a tree**, so the outline is a spanning tree: start at the hypothesis, walk out along wires in the order the map lists them, and give each claim **exactly one item**, at its first arrival. A claim with several causes does not appear twice — instead its sentence names every incoming wire. Nothing is lost and the tree stays a tree. Claims with no incoming wire at all are roots; the hypothesis is always the first of them, and on the strike branch **S** is the second.
185:**A claim with no market price** reads "no market" and then the reason, which is chosen by the claim's kind (Kent, 2026-09-17; the words live once in `spec/vocabulary.md`). A `market` claim: *"no venue quotes this claim; what you would trade is on the payoff."* An `event` or `hypothesis`: *"no venue quotes this claim."* A `not_tradeable` ending keeps **its own stored reason**, because that one is a finding rather than an absence. The tile itself says only `no market`; the reason belongs to the Inspector, the hover, and this sentence.
211:Every count comes from somewhere nameable: the **added** and **downstream** counts from `diff-view.md`'s reducer — on the strike branch that is S added, six claims downstream (H, C, B, N1, M1, M2), and R `untouched`, because the only wire that could carry the edit to R is reflexive and the diff sets those aside; the **retracted** count from UX-14, which `tiles-ports-wires.md` renders on H's tile; and **no numbers yet** said out loud rather than left as a silence.
217:Focus is **always** visible, drawn with `--focus`, on every interactive thing — tiles, chips, wires, buttons, palette rows, outline items. `outline: none` appears nowhere in the tree. Tab order follows the map's reading order, and Tab alone reaches everything.
221:**INV-12 — nothing is carried by hue alone.** Every direction of financial effect has a glyph and a sign as well as a hue; every tail risk is a hatch texture rather than a colour; every provenance is a three-step mark at the wire's tail. **The law itself lives in `color-motion-type.md`** — this chapter only depends on it, and the outline view is its strictest test: a rendering with no colour at all that still says everything.
239:| **INV-workbench.33** | For every focused claim and every press of `h` or `l`, the claim focus lands on is joined to it by a wire; focus never moves to a claim that is merely nearby on screen | `test_h_and_l_land_only_on_a_wired_neighbour` in `frontend/src/keyboard/__tests__/focusMap.test.ts`; visual review checklist line 9 (does arrow movement follow the wires?) |
245:| **INV-workbench.39** | For every claim in the world there is exactly one outline item, its sentence names every incoming wire, and the announcement names no number the world does not carry | `frontend/e2e/hormuz.spec.ts`; visual review checklist line 5 (is there a number nobody computed?) |
250:2. **Do not move focus by screen geometry**, because the tile nearest your arrow key is often not connected to the one you are on, and a map's meaning is its wires. Follow the wires, and say which wire you took.
252:4. **Do not round in the view model**, because the Inspector needs the precision the chip threw away, and a number rounded twice drifts a whole step. Carry the full number; round once, in the chip, at paint.
266:3. **Is there an announcement for ordinary focus movement?** The outline reads a claim when you land on it, but a sighted keyboard user moving quickly along wires gets only the status line. Whether that line is also an `aria-live` region, or whether that would be unbearable chatter, is untested.
269:**Decided 2026-09-17 and now in the body:** the rounding rule, both range ends, and the certainty guard (B6) · which form of the chip appears where (B6) · how `h`/`l` picks among several wires, and the status line it writes to (B2) · that navigation follows every wire including feedback ones, under the one rule in `spec/multiverse/interventions.md` (B2) · where the reason beside an empty market slot comes from (B7).

339:4. **Do not ask for one strength per combination of parents.** A proposition with five parents has thirty-two combinations; a model will happily invent thirty-two numbers, and no human can audit past three. 191:### B4 — A number that can say why
192-
193-Click the model chip on *"Brent crude settles below $68 for five sessions"* and the Inspector unrolls it (illustrative):
194-
195-```
196-prior                            .20 (.10–.35)   base rate: 4 of 19 months since 2022 in which
197-                                                 Brent crude settled below $68 for five sessions
198-+ H, the strait opens (trigger)  +1.6 push       "the war-risk premium in the price unwinds"
199-+ C, the Lloyd's war-risk
200-  premium for Gulf transits
201-  falls below 0.4% (sustain)     +0.7 push       "cheaper insurance lowers delivered cost"
202-= model                          .71 (.55–.83)
203-```
204-
205-A *push* is decision record 0005's link strength: a signed amount added on the log-odds scale — the scale on which independent influences add up instead of multiplying. Two pushes of `+1.6` and `+0.7` on a prior of `.20` land on `.71`; the propagation chapter of the multiverse part (stack 03a) spells out the arithmetic and where the range comes from. The rule this chapter enforces is narrower: no line of that list may be a number whose owner cannot be named.
206-
207-### B5 — Two significant figures, always, and only at the last moment
208-
209-`p = 0.6134` is what the domain stores, sends over the wire, and replays. `.61` is what the chip shows. `p = 0.6134, lo = 0.4471, hi = 0.7522` displays as `.61 (.45–.75)`. A chip is never permitted to show `.6134`; the rendering test in the frontend checks exactly that, and that the range is never omitted.
210-
211----
212-
213-## INVARIANTS
214-
215-Each is written *for all inputs drawn from generator S, statement P holds*, and names the automated test that checks it.
216-
217-Generators live in `backend/tests/strategies.py`: `beliefs()`, `propositions()` and `graphs()` produce random beliefs, propositions and maps that are **valid by construction**. Local numbers are unique across the whole of `spec/graph/`: this chapter uses `INV-graph.12`–`INV-graph.14`, [`proposition.md`](proposition.md) uses `INV-graph.9`–`INV-graph.11`, and the lower numbers belong to [`link.md`](link.md) and [`validity.md`](validity.md).
218-
219-### INV-graph.12 — Honest numbers *(refines INV-7)*
220-
221-- For every belief drawn from `backend/tests/strategies.py::beliefs()`: `0 ≤ lo ≤ p ≤ hi ≤ 1`.
222-- For every three floats drawn from the `hypothesis` property-testing library's own `floats()` and every owner drawn from its `sampled_from(("model", "user", "market"))` — that pair is `backend/tests/strategies.py::raw_belief_fields()`: constructing a `Belief` from them either produces one satisfying that chain of inequalities, or raises. There is no third outcome, and no silent clamping to fit.
223-- For every graph drawn from `backend/tests/strategies.py::graphs()` driven through a random sequence of interventions by the state machine `GraphEditMachine`: after **every** step, every belief on every proposition still satisfies it.
224-- **Tests:** `test_belief_bounds_at_construction` — introduced by this chapter, **stack 02**. And `test_belief_bounds_after_any_sequence` — named in decision record 0008's invariant table, driven by `GraphEditMachine`, **stack 03a**, because nothing applies an intervention until then.
225-
226-### INV-graph.13 — Three voices, never merged *(refines INV-11)*
227-
228-Two checks, one test name.
229-
230-- **Over our own source code.** Here the thing quantified over is not generated data but every module under `backend/src/katalyst/domain/`, walked at test time — a static check with a fixed, finite input, which is why it names no generator. For every function defined in any of those modules: none takes beliefs of two different owners — two or more `Belief` parameters, or one `Beliefs` — and returns a `float`, a `Belief`, or a structure containing either. Checked by walking the syntax tree of every module under `domain/` and reading its type annotations, the same technique as the import-boundary test `test_domain_imports_nothing_impure`. **Stack 02.**
231-- **Over generated data.** For every proposition drawn from `propositions()` that has all three slots filled, and every belief drawn from `beliefs()` re-owned to `user`: applying a `believe` intervention with that belief leaves `beliefs.model` and `beliefs.market` byte-identical, and changes only `beliefs.user`. **Stack 03a**, since applying an intervention is stack 03a's work; [`../multiverse/interventions.md`](../multiverse/interventions.md) states the same guarantee from the other side as `test_believe_touches_only_user_belief`.
232-- **Test:** `test_beliefs_never_merged` — named in decision record 0004's confirmation list. Decision record 0010 adds its outward-facing twin, `test_market_belief_never_merged`, which extends the source-code check to `api/` and to the thesis-card builder.
233-
234-### INV-graph.14 — Every belief sits in the slot that matches its owner
235-
236-- For every proposition drawn from `propositions()`: `prior.owner` and `beliefs.model.owner` are `"model"`; `beliefs.user.owner`, where the slot is filled, is `"user"`; `beliefs.market.owner`, where filled, is `"market"`.

1	/**
2	 * How big a tile is, and how far the map may be zoomed.
3	 *
4	 * The automatic layout has to know how big every tile is *before* the browser
5	 * has drawn one — it works out where the tiles go from the shape of the map
6	 * alone, and it cannot wait for measurements. So a tile's height is computed
7	 * here, from the claim's own content, by a plain function of plain data. That
8	 * keeps the layout a pure function of the map: the same map lays out the same
9	 * way every time, and the layout can be tested without a browser.
10	 *
11	 * The block heights below were measured once in the browser against the stored
12	 * example and are written down rather than read back at run time. If the tile's
13	 * stylesheet changes a line height or a gap, these change with it — and the
14	 * check for that is visual: a tile whose numbers are wrong has a gap at the
15	 * bottom or loses its last line.
16	 */
17	
18	import type { ClaimView } from "../world";
19	
20	/** How wide a tile is. Settled: 280 pixels, and measurable on any screenshot. */
21	export const TILE_WIDTH = 280;
22	
23	/**
24	 * How tall a tile may be, at the least and at the most.
25	 *
26	 * "Clamped height" is a floor and a ceiling with the content deciding in
27	 * between — not one height for every tile. The floor is what a tile holding
28	 * only a heading, a one-line claim and the three belief chips comes to; the
29	 * ceiling is what the densest tile in the stored example needs, which is the
30	 * hypothesis, with a three-line claim, a reason and two evidence clippings.
31	 * Both are on the eight-pixel grid.
32	 */
33	export const TILE_MIN_HEIGHT = 152;
34	export const TILE_MAX_HEIGHT = 272;
35	
36	/* ---- The blocks a tile is made of, in pixels --------------------------- *
37	 * Measured in the browser, at the type sizes and line heights `tile.css`
38	 * sets. Every one of them is a height the browser actually produced. */
39	
40	/** Top and bottom padding together: twelve pixels each. */
41	const PADDING = 24;
42	
43	/** The gap between one block and the next. */
44	const GAP = 8;
45	
46	/** The heading row: what kind of claim this is, and when it settles. */
47	const HEADER = 21;
48	
49	/**
50	 * One line of the claim, at fifteen pixels over a line height of 1.35.
51	 *
52	 * Rounded up wherever it is used, never down: a line that is given a quarter of
53	 * a pixel less than it needs loses the bottom of its descenders.
54	 */
55	const CLAIM_LINE = 20.25;
56	
57	/** The three belief chips: owner, number and range, with the rule above them. */
58	const BELIEF_RAIL = 67;
59	
60	/**
61	 * The line a dead end prints saying why nothing here can be traded. Clamped to
62	 * two lines, and the only reason any tile prints for itself.
63	 */
64	const FINDING = 35;
65	
66	/** One evidence clipping, and the gap between two of them. */
67	const CLIPPING = 21;
68	const CLIPPING_GAP = 4;
69	
70	/**
71	 * Roughly how many characters of the claim fit on one line.
72	 *
73	 * The claim has 256 pixels to wrap in (244 on the two tiles whose outline cuts
74	 * into one side) and is set at fifteen pixels in the interface face, whose
75	 * average character is about eight pixels wide — so about thirty-three.
76	 *
77	 * It is an estimate, and it is safe to be one because the same number decides
78	 * both how tall the tile is and how many lines the claim is allowed to show.
79	 * The two cannot disagree: if the estimate is generous the tile has a little
80	 * room to spare, and if it is mean the claim stops one line earlier than it
81	 * might have. Neither case can push a word out of the box.
82	 */
83	const CLAIM_CHARACTERS_PER_LINE = 33;
84	
85	/** The most lines of the claim a tile ever shows. The rest lives in the panel. */
86	const CLAIM_MAX_LINES = 3;
87	
88	/**
89	 * How many lines of the claim this tile shows.
90	 *
91	 * @param claim The claim, in the words the map serves it in.
92	 */
93	export function claimLines(claim: string): number {
94	  const wanted = Math.ceil(claim.length / CLAIM_CHARACTERS_PER_LINE);
95	  return Math.min(CLAIM_MAX_LINES, Math.max(1, wanted));
96	}
97	
98	/** Round up to the eight-pixel grid the whole interface sits on. */
99	function toGrid(height: number): number {
100	  return Math.ceil(height / 8) * 8;
101	}
102	
103	/**
104	 * How tall this claim's tile is: as tall as its own content, on the grid, and
105	 * inside the floor and the ceiling.
106	 *
107	 * @param claim The claim the tile is for.
108	 */
109	export function tileHeight(claim: ClaimView): number {
110	  const blocks: number[] = [HEADER, Math.ceil(CLAIM_LINE * claimLines(claim.claim)), BELIEF_RAIL];
111	
112	  // The foot of the tile: the reason a slot has no number, and the evidence
113	  // clippings. It is only there when there is something to put in it — and
114	  // when the badges arrive, having one of those will put it there too.
115	  const foot: number[] = [];
116	  if (claim.kind === "not_tradeable" && claim.beliefs.market.absence !== undefined) {
117	    foot.push(FINDING);
118	  }
119	  const clippings = claim.evidence.length;
120	  if (clippings > 0) {
121	    foot.push(CLIPPING * clippings + CLIPPING_GAP * (clippings - 1));
122	  }
123	  if (foot.length > 0) {
124	    blocks.push(foot.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) + GAP * (foot.length - 1));
125	  }
126	
127	  const natural = PADDING + blocks.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) + GAP * (blocks.length - 1);
128	  return Math.min(TILE_MAX_HEIGHT, Math.max(TILE_MIN_HEIGHT, toGrid(natural)));
129	}
130	
131	/* ---- Zoom --------------------------------------------------------------- */
132	
133	/**
134	 * The smallest a word may be drawn on the reader's screen, in pixels.
135	 *
136	 * This is the rule the two zoom numbers below are worked out from, rather than
137	 * a number chosen for how it looked.
138	 */
139	const SMALLEST_READABLE_TEXT = 11;
140	
141	/** The smallest and largest of the three type sizes, as `tokens.css` sets them. */
142	const SMALLEST_TEXT = 13;
143	const LARGEST_TEXT = 22;
144	
145	/**
146	 * Below this zoom a tile stops showing everything and shows a summary instead.
147	 *
148	 * **This was 0.6, and it is now eleven over thirteen — about 0.85.** The plan
149	 * settled on 0.6 before the type scale was settled, and the two turned out not
150	 * to fit together: a full tile's smallest words are thirteen pixels, so at 0.6
151	 * zoom they arrive on the glass at under eight, which breaks the rule that
152	 * nothing is ever drawn below eleven. Eleven over thirteen is the exact zoom at
153	 * which thirteen-pixel type lands at eleven pixels, so a full tile is only ever
154	 * shown at or above it, and below it the summary takes over — which sets every
155	 * word in the largest size and so clears the floor all the way down.
156	 */
157	export const SUMMARY_BELOW_ZOOM = SMALLEST_READABLE_TEXT / SMALLEST_TEXT;
158	
159	/**
160	 * How far out the map may be zoomed.
161	 *
162	 * The summary sets every word it draws in the largest of the three type sizes,
163	 * so the floor is the one zoom at which that size arrives at eleven pixels:
164	 * eleven over twenty-two, which is a half.
165	 */
166	export const SMALLEST_ZOOM = SMALLEST_READABLE_TEXT / LARGEST_TEXT;
167	
168	/** How far in the map may be zoomed. Past this a tile is merely large. */
169	export const LARGEST_ZOOM = 1.4;
170	
171	/**
172	 * The smallest type size a tile draws at this zoom, in pixels, before the map's
173	 * own scaling is applied.
174	 *
175	 * Multiply it by the zoom and you have what lands on the reader's screen, which
176	 * is what `layout.test.ts` checks never falls below eleven.
177	 *
178	 * @param zoom How far the map is zoomed in, where 1 is life size.
179	 */
180	export function smallestTextAt(zoom: number): number {
181	  return zoom < SUMMARY_BELOW_ZOOM ? LARGEST_TEXT : SMALLEST_TEXT;
182	}
183	
184	/** The smallest a word is ever drawn on the reader's screen, in pixels. */
185	export const TEXT_FLOOR = SMALLEST_READABLE_TEXT;
186	
187	/** How many tiles a single layer may show before the rest are collapsed into one. */

7:Three chapters sit next to this one and are not repeated here: `tiles-ports-wires.md` says what is inside a tile and how a wire is drawn, `color-motion-type.md` carries the colour law and the motion budget, and `diff-view.md` says how two worlds are painted once they share a coordinate space. This chapter owns only **where things go and how big they are**.
35:| `nodePlacement.strategy: NETWORK_SIMPLEX` | Decides each tile's position **within** its column so that wires come out as straight as possible. Straight wires are short wires; short wires cross less |
37:| `spacing.nodeNodeBetweenLayers: 120` | 120 pixels of gutter between one column and the next — enough room for a midpoint chip and an origin mark on the wire without the chip touching a tile |
51:   *  (`tiles-ports-wires.md` owns the height rule). */
53:  /** Every wire. `reflexive` wires are marked here and set aside before layering. */
54:  wires: { id: string; from: string; to: string; reflexive: boolean }[];
79:  detail: "summary" | "full";
108:R sits in column 1, tight against B, because its only live arrow is `R → B`. Nothing pulls it further left, and network simplex does not leave a wire longer than it has to be.
138:Layering asks what can move, so it reads the map with `B → R` removed. That is also why R comes out `untouched` on the strike branch. `test_a_feedback_arrow_never_carries_a_change` fails loudly the day stack 06 unrolls feedback arrows in time, and points at the one sentence to change. **How that wire looks — the loop, the lag chip reading "14 days" — is `tiles-ports-wires.md`.** This chapter only guarantees that the wire exists, that it never decides a column, and that removing it can never fail: INV-6 (no loops except through reflexive arrows, each with a delay greater than zero) is already enforced in the engine, so a map that reaches the canvas is one the loop check has passed.
148:**A collapsed claim's wires do not disappear.** A wire that vanishes is a state a user cannot trace, which is the second veto. The wires of the hidden claims attach to the "+n more" tile. *How they bundle is still open — see Open questions.*
157:| **Zoom floor 0.5** | 11 ÷ 22 = 0.5 | A summary tile's type is `--text-lg`, 22 px. At 0.5 it lands at exactly 11 px. You cannot zoom out past that, because the next pixel out is unreadable |
161:Below the summary threshold a tile paints its **summary**: the claim and the three belief chips inside the same kind silhouette, nothing else. The outline never goes — it is the tile's shape, and dropping it would lose the claim's kind at exactly the zoom where you are scanning for one. Above it the tile paints in full — claim, chips, evidence clippings, resolve-by date (`tiles-ports-wires.md`).
163:**The honest cost.** Measured on the Hormuz map: on a 1440-pixel-wide window the first frame is summary tiles, because `fitView` cannot fit the map any larger. At 1600 wide it is full tiles, at about 11.4 pixels — legible, and only just. A narrow window therefore opens on summaries and you zoom in to read. That is the price of the promise, and it is cheaper than the alternative, which is text nobody can read at a zoom the interface offered them.
170:| **Mid** | Wiring and belief chips | This stack — between the 0.5 floor and 0.85, the summary tile |
175:A diff shows the base map and the branch at the same time. Both are laid out **once, together, as one graph** — every claim in either world, every wire in either world — and then painted twice in those same coordinates. One layout, two paintings. **How they are painted is `diff-view.md`.**
222:| **INV-workbench.27** | For every zoom from the 0.5 floor to the ceiling, the smallest rendered type size × the zoom is at least 11 — below ≈0.85 because the tile has switched to its summary, above it because 13 × 0.85 already clears 11 | `test_no_text_lands_under_eleven_pixels_at_any_zoom` in `layout.test.ts`, a sweep over the whole zoom range; visual review checklist line 7 (is any text below 11 pixels?) |
231:3. **Do not let text land under 11 pixels on the glass**, because an unreadable label is worse than no label. Switch the tile to its summary at 0.85 and stop the zoom at 0.5 — and do not counter-scale the text to dodge the rule, because a tile whose contents ignore the zoom stops being a picture of the map.
233:5. **Do not hide a wire when its tile collapses into "+n more"**, because a wire that vanishes is a state nobody can trace — the second veto. Attach it to the "+n more" tile.
242:1. **How do a collapsed claim's wires bundle?** One thick wire to the "+n more" tile with a count on it, or n thin wires all landing on the same socket? The first is legible; the second is literal. The chapter requires only that no wire disappears. *(Which seven survive, and what activating "+n more" does, were* **Decided 2026-09-17** *— both are in B5.)*
243:2. **Should 280 and 120 become tokens?** Every other pixel number in the product lives in `frontend/src/styles/tokens.css`. The tile width and the column gutter currently would not. Adding them touches a file this stack's wire agent owns (the new colour block), so it is a coordination question, not a design one.
